strengths: Novel and well-motivated application of mechanistic interpretability: the paper locates specialized typographic attention heads in CLIP and demonstrates a causal link between their cls-token attention and typographic vulnerability via controlled attention-pattern interventions (Fig. 5), which goes beyond correlational probing analyses.

Practically attractive training-free defense: circuit ablation requires no finetuning, scales to billion-parameter models (ViT-B through ViT-BigG) on consumer hardware, and yields sparse circuits (4-10% of heads), with released 'dyslexic CLIP' model family enhancing reproducibility and practical impact.

Multi-scale empirical validation: robustness gains (up to +19.6% on ImageNet-100-Typo, +13-32% on real-world attack datasets) are consistent across five model sizes, with minimal degradation on standard benchmarks (typically within ±1%), and additional evaluation on RTA-100, Disentangling, and PAINT-DS showing the circuit generalizes beyond the synthetic construction.

Good supporting analyses: layer-wise probe emergence (Fig. 2), intrinsic dimensionality analysis (App. A), attention-sink behavior of circuit heads (App. B), and transparency about limitations (cls-token-only intervention, misuse potential).
weaknesses: Baseline comparison is thin: only Defense-Prefix is compared, and only on ViT-L. Other directly relevant defenses cited in related work — SAE-based steering [22], weight interpolation [19], projection-matrix approaches [18] — are not compared, making the 'competitive with state-of-the-art' claim only partially supported (and DP actually outperforms the method on most typographic benchmarks in Table 4).

Missing key ablation/control: there is no random-head-ablation baseline of equal circuit size to demonstrate that the identified typographic circuit is specifically responsible for robustness gains, rather than generic head ablation in later layers. Sensitivity to the ε threshold (0.01) and the 5% control-split choice is also not analyzed.

Circularity concerns: the circuit is constructed using ImageNet-100-Typo, and the headline improvement (+19.6%) is reported on the same dataset; while real-world attack datasets mitigate this, the largest gains may partly reflect construction-set fit.

Evaluation scope is limited to zero-shot classification. The abstract and introduction motivate the work with jailbreaks and harmful generation in VLMs/diffusion pipelines, but no experiments support robustness in those settings, and the authors themselves acknowledge the cls-token-only intervention may not protect architectures (LLaVA, IP-Adapter) that rely on spatial tokens — weakening the 'drop-in replacement for safety-critical applications' claim.
Small real-world attack evaluation sets (180-1100 images) with no variance/significance reporting; several reported gains rest on modest sample sizes.

Presentation issues: multiple typos and grammatical errors ('behaivor', 'dislexic', 'int the image', 'we choose ε = 0.01 by and set'), inconsistent naming (Typograhic/dislexic), and Eq. (6) as rendered is unclear; these reduce polish and could introduce ambiguity in the core method definition.

The Typographic Attention Score relies on a fixed-position synthetic dataset (Unsplash-Typo), and the generality of the score to arbitrary text placements and real-world typography is argued only indirectly.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: typographic attacks on CLIP are a real vulnerability for deployed multimodal systems, and a training-free defense is a meaningful alternative to finetuning-based defenses.

The mechanistic analysis (layer-wise linear probes, Typographic Attention Score, attention-sink behavior in App. B) is a genuine interpretability contribution, and the attention-manipulation experiment (Fig. 5, Eq. 8) provides causal evidence linking the identified heads to typographic vulnerability rather than mere correlation.

Evaluation covers five OpenCLIP model scales (ViT-B to ViT-BigG) and four typographic attack datasets (RTA-100, Disentangling, PAINT-DS, ImageNet-100-Typo), showing consistent robustness gains (up to ~19.6%) with small (<1%) degradation on standard benchmarks.

The paper is candid about limitations: the method only protects the cls token, so it may not transfer to VLMs that consume spatial tokens, and it discusses potential misuse of the findings. Releasing the dyslexic model family aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Insufficient baseline comparison for the headline claim. The abstract claims the approach 'remains competitive with current state-of-the-art typographic defenses that rely on finetuning,' but the only baseline is Defense-Prefix, evaluated on a single model (ViT-L), and it actually outperforms the proposed method on most typographic benchmarks (Table 4). Other cited defenses (weight interpolation [19], projection matrices [18], SAE steering [22]) are not compared at all.

Methodological ambiguities undermine confidence. The Typographic Attention Score (Eq. 6) is stated to lie in [0,1], yet the reported scores and heatmaps range far beyond that (e.g., 79.9, 'up to x3 the mean'); the normalization and the role of ||A*|| are unclear. Eq. 8 manipulates attention patterns directly, but attention patterns are computed from hidden states, so the implementation of this intervention (recomputing values? overriding softmax output?) is not specified.

The circuit construction arguably involves dataset-specific tuning despite the 'training-free' framing: the score is computed on synthetic typography at a fixed position (bottom-center of Unsplash-Typo), and circuit selection uses a labeled ImageNet-100-Typo variant plus an ImageNet-100 validation split. The generalization of the score to typography at arbitrary positions, fonts, and real-world layouts is not analyzed in depth.

Limited practical scope: the defense suppresses all text recognition, making models 'dyslexic.' The paper's own discussion concedes that systems using spatial tokens (LLaVA, IP-Adapter) remain vulnerable, and only zero-shot classification is evaluated, not retrieval, diffusion conditioning, or VLM jailbreak settings, despite these being motivating use cases in the introduction.

Evaluation rigor gaps: no variance across seeds, no confidence intervals or statistical tests for the reported deltas (some of which, e.g., +0.05%/+0.06% in Table 3, are likely within noise), and epsilon = 0.01 is chosen without ablation or justification.

The manuscript is not polished: numerous typos and grammatical errors ('behaivor', 'Typograhic', 'dislexic', 'cls tokent', 'infered', 'the the typography region'), inconsistent capitalization (Imagenet/ImageNet), and a method section (Algorithm 1) whose break-on-first-violation logic is not analyzed (e.g., what happens with score ties or non-monotonic accuracy curves).

Novelty is moderate: head ablation, linear probing, and attention-pattern interventions are standard mechanistic-interpretability tools; the contribution is their application to a known failure mode, with the main new element being the attention-based score. Related work on attention-based attack detection [30] is acknowledged as the direct foundation.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: the paper combines mechanistic analysis (layer-wise linear probes, Typographic Attention Score) with a practical training-free defense based on circuit ablation, which is a genuinely novel angle compared to existing finetuning-based typographic defenses.

Strong causal evidence: the attention-pattern manipulation experiment (Fig. 5, Eq. 8) directly demonstrates the causal role of the identified circuit heads in typographic attacks, going beyond correlational probing.

Comprehensive scale and dataset coverage: circuits are constructed and validated across five OpenCLIP model sizes (ViT-B to ViT-BigG) and evaluated on multiple real-world typographic attack datasets (RTA-100, Disentangling, PAINT-DS), not only the synthetic ImageNet-100-Typo.

Favorable trade-off: consistent robustness gains (up to ~19.6%) with less than ~1% degradation on non-typographic benchmarks, and the training-free approach is competitive with Defense-Prefix, which requires training and generalizes worse to non-typographic datasets.
Practical reproducibility: model release of dyslexic CLIP variants, use of open tooling (OpenCLIP, Prisma), consumer-grade hardware, and a dedicated reproducibility appendix.
Honest discussion of limitations (spatial-token-based VLMs not covered) and potential misuse.
weaknesses: Greedy circuit construction is methodologically fragile: the algorithm breaks permanently at the first head whose ablation incurs a ΔAcc ≥ ε drop, so all lower-ranked heads are never considered; there is no discussion of ordering sensitivity, no comparison to alternative selection strategies (e.g., exhaustive search within top-k, backward elimination), and no variance analysis over multiple runs or random seeds.

Potential confound in the Typographic Attention Score: heads are identified using Unsplash-Typo with text fixed at the bottom-center of images, so high-scoring heads may partly reflect spatial-position bias rather than typography selectivity per se; the paper does not directly control for this (e.g., randomizing text position when computing T_i,ℓ).

Baseline comparison is thin: only Defense-Prefix on a single model size (ViT-L) is compared; other relevant defenses mentioned in related work — weight interpolation [19], projection matrices [18], and SAE-based steering [22] — are not empirically compared, weakening the 'competitive with state-of-the-art' claim.

Evaluation of retained text understanding is missing: the defense deliberately removes text recognition, but benchmarks (Aircraft, Food-101, ImageNet-100) contain almost no text; the effect on genuinely text-bearing inputs (memes, screenshots, watermarked or captioned images) is untested, which matters for the 'drop-in replacement for safety-critical applications' claim.

The central quantitative claim (up to 19.6%) is on the authors' own synthetic ImageNet-100-Typo; gains on real-world attack datasets are more modest (e.g., +6.1% RTA-100 for ViT-L), and single-run results without confidence intervals or significance testing.
Adaptive attacks are acknowledged (attackers could boost spatial attention of circuit heads) but not evaluated, so robustness claims are limited to non-adaptive threat models.

Numerous presentation issues: typos ('Typograhic', 'behaivor', 'dislexic', 'the a Imagenet-100', 'we choose ϵ = 0.01 by and set'), a poorly specified Eq. 6 (the indicator cancels in the fraction, making the formula confusing as written), and some claims stated too strongly relative to evidence (e.g., 'first work to address typographic vulnerabilities through causal interventions' given related SAE steering work).

strengths: Novel contribution: first gradient-free, mechanistic-interpretability-based defense against typographic attacks in CLIP, positioned clearly against existing fine-tuning/projection/prefix-based defenses.

Strong mechanistic analysis: the paper traces typographic understanding across layers with linear probes, introduces a Typographic Attention Score to localize specialized attention heads, and validates causality through controlled attention-sink manipulation (Eq. 10), not just correlation.

Comprehensive empirical validation across model scales (ViT-B to ViT-bigG, up to billion parameters), multiple typographic benchmarks (real and synthetic), and a clinically relevant medical use case (WhyLesionCLIP melanoma detection), where attacks reduce accuracy by up to ~22% and Dyslexify recovers up to ~19%.

Favorable robustness-utility trade-off: up to +22% robustness on typographic benchmarks with <1% degradation on standard ImageNet-100; sparse circuits (4.5-10.1% of heads) support the claim of targeted intervention.

Honest and thorough limitations analysis: OCR degradation quantified (Table 6), runtime/memory comparison against Defense-Prefix, and a candid discussion of the strong OCR+blur baseline and restricted cls-token scope.
Good reproducibility posture: anonymized open-source code, model release, detailed dataset descriptions, and reproducibility/ethics statements.
weaknesses: The strongest baseline (OCR detection + blurring, Appendix J) actually outperforms Dyslexify on ImageNet-100-Typo across all model sizes, yet this comparison is relegated to the appendix. The main-text baseline comparison (Table 3) covers only Defense-Prefix, so the headline claim of being 'competitive with state-of-the-art defenses' needs more careful qualification in light of this stronger baseline.

The argument for why adaptive attacks are infeasible is unconvincing: typographic attacks are claimed to be 'inherently non-differentiable', but attackers could use gradient-free search (fonts, sizes, placements) or surrogate models to optimize text against the ablated circuit, especially since the paper itself notes adversarial inputs could increase spatial attention of heads in C. This is a standard requirement for adversarial-robustness claims.

Potential evaluation leakage: circuits are constructed using ImageNet-100-typo and then evaluated partly on the same dataset's split; while gains transfer to other benchmarks, the headline 22.06% figure is partly on construction data.

Generalization to the settings that matter most is limited by design: the defense only protects the cls token, while LLaVA/IP-adapter-style applications consume spatial tokens; the medical/zero-shot use cases are relatively narrow relative to the safety-critical-deployment claims in the abstract.

The Typographic Attention Score is validated on a synthetic localized dataset (text at a fixed bottom-center position); robustness of head localization to variable text positions and real-world typography (beyond small benchmark sets like the 180-image Disentangling set) could be examined more thoroughly.

Presentation issues: several typos and incomplete fields ('Poject page:', 'gadient-free', 'constrast'), and some figures (e.g., Fig. 3 heatmap, Fig. 5) are hard to read or under-explained; Eq. 10's normalization notation is somewhat ambiguous.

strengths: The mechanistic analysis (layer-wise linear probes, Typographic Attention Score, attention-sink observation, and the alpha-intervention in Fig. 5) provides a reasonably convincing causal story for why typographic attacks work on CLIP's cls token, which is the paper's most interesting contribution.

Evaluation spans model scales from ViT-B to ViT-bigG, multiple typographic attack benchmarks (RTA-100, Disentangling, PAINT), and includes a medical use case (WhyLesionCLIP), showing the method is not confined to a single model.

The paper is unusually honest in places: it discloses that the simple OCR+blur baseline outperforms Dyslexify on absolute robustness (Tables 8-9), quantifies the OCR capability loss (Table 6), and reports the cls-token-only limitation regarding VLMs.
Gradient-free nature and favorable runtime/VRAM footprint (Section I) make the method practical and scalable to large models where finetuning defenses fail.
weaknesses: Selection/evaluation contamination: the typographic circuit C is constructed and its stopping criterion evaluated on ImageNet-100-typo, and the headline robustness numbers (Fig. 4, Table 1, +22.06%) appear to be reported on this same dataset ('ImageNet-100-typo's train set'). This risks inflating the central claim, and a held-out circuit-construction protocol should have been used.

The adaptive-attack justification is not persuasive. The authors claim adaptive attacks are infeasible because typographic attacks are 'inherently non-differentiable', but the real vulnerability is that the circuit is identified using synthetic typographic data with only three fonts at random locations; an attacker using different fonts, placements, sizes, or blurred/occluded text could plausibly bypass the ablated heads. Robustness to these shifts is not studied.

The paper's own OCR+blur baseline consistently beats Dyslexify on typographic robustness with negligible accuracy cost, substantially weakening the practical argument for the method. The rebuttal (no inference-time cost, mechanistic insight) is qualitative; the practical case for choosing Dyslexify over this simple baseline is not established.

Baseline coverage is thin: only Defense-Prefix is compared. Established defenses such as weight patching/interpolation (Ilharco et al., 2022, cited but not compared) and SAE-based steering (Joseph et al., 2025, cited but not compared) are missing, making it hard to judge the competitiveness of the approach.

The medical experiment has limited significance: zero-shot melanoma accuracies are low (e.g., 31.99% on BCN20k), and the threat model (text labels overlaid on dermoscopic images at the ImageNet scale) is quite artificial relative to how clinical systems would actually be attacked.

The defense is restricted to the cls token residual stream; the authors themselves acknowledge that LLaVA-style models and IP-adapters rely on spatial tokens, so the applicability to the VLM settings where typographic jailbreaking matters most remains unaddressed.

Presentation issues undermine polish: 'Poject page:' and 'Code:' are left empty in the abstract, and there are multiple typos ('gadient-free', 'casual nature', 'behaivor'). Several figures (e.g., Figs. 11-15 heatmaps) are dense and hard to read; the code appears anonymized but inaccessible to reviewers.

strengths: Novel and practically valuable contribution: a gradient-free, inference-time defense against typographic attacks based on circuit-level ablation, which is genuinely different from existing fine-tuning/prefix/projection-based defenses and scales to billion-parameter models on consumer hardware.

Strong mechanistic analysis: the paper goes beyond showing a defense works by (i) locating when typographic understanding emerges across layers via linear probes, (ii) introducing the Typographic Attention Score to identify specific attention heads, (iii) connecting these heads to attention-sink behavior, and (iv) providing causal evidence through attention-pattern manipulation (Fig. 5) and head ablation.

Comprehensive empirical validation across model scales (ViT-B to ViT-bigG) and multiple typographic benchmarks (real-world: RTA-100, Disentangling, PAINT; synthetic: -typo variants), with large robustness gains (up to +31%) and minimal clean-accuracy degradation (<1% in most cases).

Compelling safety-critical use case: demonstrating that typographic attacks can reduce melanoma detection accuracy by up to 22% and that Dyslexify mitigates this, strengthening the practical significance of the work.

Unusually transparent limitations: the authors honestly report OCR capability degradation, the OCR+blur baseline that outperforms Dyslexify in absolute robustness, and the limited applicability to models using spatial tokens; runtime, memory, and ablation studies are documented in the appendix.
Model release of dyslexic CLIP checkpoints and anonymized code supports reproducibility and adoption.
weaknesses: Limited baseline comparison: only Defense-Prefix is directly compared, despite several other defenses existing in the literature (Materzynska et al.'s projection matrix, Ilharco et al.'s weight-space fine-tuning, SAE-based steering of Joseph et al.). Claims of competitiveness with 'state-of-the-art' defenses rest on a single baseline.

No adaptive attack evaluation: while the authors argue typographic attacks are non-differentiable, search-based or heuristic adaptive attacks tailored to circumvent head ablation (e.g., placing text to avoid circuit-head attention) are plausible and untested; the Misuse Potential paragraph itself concedes such attacks may exist.

The circuit construction requires labeled typographic data and iterative evaluation on ImageNet-100-typo; the generalization of a circuit built on synthetic overlays to arbitrary real-world typography (fonts, layouts, languages) is only indirectly assessed via the real typographic datasets, which are themselves Post-it-based.

Presentation quality issues undermine polish: empty 'Project page:' and 'Code:' placeholders in the submission, and multiple typos ('Poject', 'gadient-free', 'casual nature' instead of causal, 'behaivor', 'responding to' instead of corresponding to), including an incomplete discussion in Section 5.2.1.

Non-typographic clean evaluation is limited to only three datasets (Aircraft, Food-101, ImageNet-100); a broader zero-shot suite would better substantiate the claim that general visual capabilities are preserved.

The core phenomenon (CLIP's typographic sensitivity) was identified by Goh et al. (2021) and defenses exist; the main novelty lies in the causal localization and ablation method, which some reviewers may view as an incremental application of activation-level intervention to a known vulnerability.

The claimed '22.06% improvement' in the abstract is the maximum gain on one synthetic benchmark; gains vary considerably across datasets (e.g., +3.45% on Aircraft-T), so headline numbers slightly overstate typical performance.
